headings.title: Introduction to Food Nutrients
headings.content: Food nutrients are chemical substances found in food that every living human body needs to survive, grow, repair itself, and maintain daily health. Without a steady supply of these substances, the human body cannot produce energy or build new tissues. Nurses study nutrition to understand how what a patient eats directly impacts their healing process, immune response, and overall physical condition. Nutrients are generally divided into two main categories depending on how much of them the body requires: macronutrients, which are needed in large amounts, and micronutrients, which are needed in much smaller quantities. Both groups work together to keep every organ system functioning smoothly.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content:
Macronutrients form the bulk of our daily diet and provide the energy and structural materials necessary for life. 

- **Carbohydrates**: These are the body's main and fastest source of energy, broken down primarily into glucose to fuel the brain and muscles.
- **Proteins**: Composed of amino acids, proteins are essential for building, repairing, and maintaining tissues like muscles, skin, and organs, as well as supporting immune function.
- **Fats (Lipids)**: Fats offer a concentrated reserve of stored energy, protect vital internal organs, insulate the body against cold, and help absorb fat-soluble vitamins.

A common misconception is that all fats are harmful; however, healthy fats from plants and fish are actually vital for proper cellular health and hormone production.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content:
Even though the body only needs small amounts of micronutrients, they are absolutely critical for regulating chemical reactions, supporting immune defenses, and maintaining healthy bones and blood.

- **Vitamins**: Organic compounds like vitamin C and the B-complex group that help enzymes function properly, boost immunity, and maintain normal cellular metabolism.
- **Minerals**: Inorganic elements like iron, calcium, and potassium that build strong bones, transmit nerve impulses, and maintain fluid balance.

A deficiency in just one of these tiny elements can lead to major clinical problems, such as iron-deficiency anemia or bone-weakening conditions like osteoporosis.

headings.title: The Vital Role of Water in Human Nutrition
headings.content: Water is often overlooked as a nutrient, yet it is the most critical substance for human survival. The adult human body is made up of roughly 60% water. It acts as a universal solvent where all cellular chemical reactions take place. Water transports dissolved nutrients and oxygen to cells, flushes out metabolic waste products through the kidneys, and regulates internal body temperature through sweating and respiration. When fluid intake drops below fluid loss, dehydration sets in, quickly leading to confusion, low blood pressure, and impaired organ function.

headings.title: Dietary Fiber and Its Digestive Functions
headings.content: Dietary fiber is a type of carbohydrate found in plant foods that the human body cannot digest or break down into glucose. Instead of being absorbed, it passes relatively intact through the stomach and small intestine. Fiber is split into two main types: soluble fiber, which dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance that helps lower cholesterol and blood sugar, and insoluble fiber, which adds bulk to stool and speeds up transit time through the colon. Eating enough fiber prevents constipation, supports a healthy gut microbiome, and lowers the risk of developing chronic bowel disorders.

headings.title: Digestion, Absorption, and Metabolism of Nutrients
headings.content: The food we eat must be transformed before the body can use it. Digestion begins in the mouth with chewing and salivary enzymes, continues in the stomach with strong acids, and finishes in the small intestine where digestive juices from the pancreas and liver break food down into tiny molecules. Absorption happens mainly across the walls of the small intestine, where nutrients pass directly into the bloodstream or lymphatic system. Once absorbed, these molecules undergo metabolism—a complex set of chemical pathways where they are either burned for immediate energy or stored for future use in the body.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Dietary Guidelines in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Nurses play a frontline role in identifying nutritional problems through regular patient assessments. This involves taking a dietary history, checking height and weight, calculating Body Mass Index (BMI), and watching for clinical signs of malnutrition such as muscle wasting or poor wound healing. Nurses use established dietary guidelines and food guides to educate patients on eating balanced meals containing appropriate proportions of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and micronutrients. Proper nutritional guidance helps prevent chronic lifestyle diseases like obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, supporting faster recovery and better long-term health outcomes.
